title: Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO): The Ultimate Clinical Guide
summary: BRVO is the second most common retinal vascular disease after diabetic retinopathy, typically occurring at arteriovenous crossings. This guide covers the pathophysiology, evidence-based management (Anti-VEGF/Laser), and landmark clinical trials like BRAVO and VIBRANT.

branches: Second most common retinal vascular disease
Primary cause of vision loss: Macular Edema (ME)

sections.title: Systemic & Ocular Risk Factors
content: Age (most significant factor)
Systemic Hypertension (present in 60-70% of cases)
Hyperlipidemia and Obesity
Diabetes Mellitus (though more linked to DR)
Cigarette Smoking
Glaucoma or elevated Intraocular Pressure (IOP)
Hypercoagulable states (Protein C/S deficiency, Factor V Leiden) - especially in patients <50

sections.title: Etiology & Pathophysiology
content: Step 1: Artery and vein share a common adventitial sheath at crossing points.
Step 2: Thickened arterial wall (atherosclerosis) compresses the vein.
Step 3: Turbulence and endothelial damage lead to thrombus formation.
Step 4: Venous pressure rises, leading to fluid leakage (Edema) and hemorrhage.
Step 5: Capillary non-perfusion leads to ischemia and VEGF release.
Step 6: High VEGF levels drive Macular Edema and Neovascularization.

rows: Involvement of superior or inferior half

sections.title: Clinical Presentation Checklist
content: Sudden, painless unilateral vision loss
Metamorphopsia (due to macular edema)
Relative visual field defect (scotoma)
Sectoral flame-shaped hemorrhages
Dilated, tortuous venous system distal to crossing
Cotton wool spots in ischemic zones
Macular thickening and hard exudates

rows: Intraretinal fluid, SRF, CME, Hyperreflective foci
Delayed filling, capillary dropout, late leakage
Assess perfusion; define Ischemic vs Non-Ischemic
BP, CBC, Gluc, Lipids, PT/PTT, (Thrombophilia screen in young)

data.label: Risk of NV in Ischemic BRVO

rows: Bilateral, generalized narrowing, Grade IV = Papilledema
History of radiation, similar to DR appearance
Hemorrhages in all 4 quadrants, optic disc swelling

sections.title: Management Algorithm
content: 1. Baseline Evaluation: VA, OCT, and systemic BP check.
2. Treat Macular Edema: First-line Anti-VEGF (Ranibizumab, Aflibercept, or Bevacizumab).
3. Re-evaluate monthly: Follow 'Pro Re Nata' (PRN) or 'Treat and Extend' protocols.
4. Second-line for ME: Intravitreal Dexamethasone implant (Ozurdex) - monitor IOP.
5. Manage Ischemia: If >5 disc areas of non-perfusion, monitor closely for NV.
6. Sectoral PRP: Perform if NVE or NVD develops (based on BVOS guidelines).
7. Vitrectomy: For non-clearing Vitreous Hemorrhage or TRD.

rows: GENEVA Trial (effective but higher IOP risk)

sections.title: Landmark Clinical Trials (High Yield)
content: BVOS (1984): Established Grid Laser for ME (VA 20/40 or worse) and Scatter Laser for NV.
BRAVO (2010): Ranibizumab 0.5mg is highly effective for BRVO-ME.
VIBRANT (2014): Aflibercept 2mg monthly showed 53% gained 15+ letters vs 27% with laser.
GENEVA: Ozurdex implant provides rapid improvement, though duration is 3-4 months.
SCORE: Triamcinolone was not superior to laser for BRVO, but effective for CRVO.

content.explanation: Grid Laser: Wait 3-6 months for hemorrhage to clear; VA < 20/40. Scatter Laser: Only after NV develops, NOT prophylactically.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Sudden 'spider-web' floaters (Vitreous Hemorrhage)
Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI) - rare in BRVO but possible in HRVO
Rising IOP after Steroid Implant (Steroid Response)
Endophthalmitis signs: Pain, worsening redness, hypopyon post-injection

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: BRVO at the disc margin is usually HRVO (Hemi-Retinal Vein Occlusion).
Always check for a 'cherry red spot' if vision loss is hand-motions or worse (suspect combined occlusion).
Collateral vessels (large, loopy vessels crossing the horizontal raphe) are a sign of chronicity and should NOT be lasered.
Young patients (<50 years) with BRVO need a thorough workup for thrombophilia and inflammatory vasculitis (Sarcoid, Lupus).
Anti-VEGF is now first-line; Grid laser is reserved for cases resistant to medical therapy or where injections are contraindicated.
